Scouts are always considered alert for Notice rolls versus Stealth, ignore up to 2 points of penalties on Survival rolls to track, and on a raise gain more specific information about what they’re following. They also add +2 to Common Knowledge rolls to recall information about towns, outposts, landmarks and watering holes, people, or tribes along a particular route they’ve traveled before.

edges.name: SIDEKICK
edges.text: A character who triumphs over evil time and time again becomes an inspiration to others. Eventually, one of these young crusaders may attempt to join the hero in their epic quests. The hero gains a Novice Rank sidekick. The sidekick is a Wild Card, starts each session with two Bennies, may Advance, and has abilities that complement their mentor. The player character controls their sidekick just like any other ally, though they may occasionally cause trouble by getting captured, running into danger when they’re not supposed to, and so on. The player should be prepared for their Edge to occasionally become a Hindrance! If the sidekick dies, they aren’t replaced unless the hero chooses this Edge again. Fortunately, heroes may always spend Bennies for their sidekicks as if they had the Common Bond Edge. Sidekicks must actually take that Edge to do the same for their mentors.

edges.name: SILENT AS A CORPSE
edges.text: As long as this deader’s feet are in contact with dirt, they can move without making a sound (even if they’re wearing boots). They add +4 to Stealth where sound is the primary factor in detection. In the Weird West, most everything that’s not actually inside a building is dirt. Even the interiors to some buildings have dirt floors, such as barns, stables, poor farmsteads, and the like.

edges.name: SLEEP O’ THE DEAD
edges.text: Manitous have something of a talent for getting mortals to sleep. Harrowed with this Edge can tap into the manitous’ abilities to send a victim straight to the Land o’ Nod with a single touch. Even other Harrowed are affected. This works much like the slumber power (page 193), except it costs no Power Points, has a Range of Touch, and is enacted with an opposed Spirit roll against the target as an action. If the Harrowed wins the opposed Spirit roll, the target falls asleep for one minute, or 1d6 hours with a raise. It can’t be maintained.

edges.name: SOLDIER
edges.text: These grunts have seen hell—maybe even walked through it. From the Union or the South, or just a grudge-bearing merc, they know how to fight dirty and fight smart. They’re used to long walks and heavy loads and enduring harsh conditions. They treat their Strength as one die type higher when determining Encumbrance (page 116) and Minimum Strength to use armor, weapons, and equipment without a penalty (page 114). (This stacks with the Brawny Edge.) They also get a free reroll on Vigor rolls made to survive environmental hazards (see Hazards, page 156).

edges.name: SOUL EATER
edges.text: Nothing about the Harrowed is pleasant. If they aren’t eating something’s flesh, preferably raw and wiggling, the demon inside often goes for raw life force instead. If the Harrowed causes a Wound or more with a successful barehanded Fighting attack (including Claws if they have them), they may make a Spirit roll at −2 immediately afterward as a free action. If successful, they may heal one of their own Wounds (or a level of Fatigue, as they choose). Inflicting multiple Wounds has no additional effect.

edges.name: SPEAK WITH THE DEAD
edges.text: After death, a soul remains somewhat tethered to their remains for a while. It decays over a few months, the spiritual connection fading along with the flesh it once occupied. Harrowed with this power can tap into those connections to call forth a cadaver’s spirit and speak to it. The body’s soul is distant and confused when summoned back to speak with the Harrowed. Its mortal memories are vague and difficult to recollect. It may have a crystal clear memory of a clear summer day it spent swimming in a creek in their youth but can’t seem to recall which of their “friends” murdered them. (That means the Marshal has full control on what information the posse gets, which should be helpful but rarely give away the mystery of a good adventure!) Contact requires touch and the corpse can’t have been dead longer than the Harrowed’s Smarts die in months. Once contact is initiated, the Marshal rolls a d6. On a 2–6, the spirit is dragged forth and answers a few questions before it’s pulled back into the Hunting Grounds and can’t be summoned again until the next full moon. On a 1, a manitou responds instead, pretending to be the corpse’s spirit, and causes as much mischief as possible!

edges.name: SPIDER
edges.text: In a world filled with terrors and abominations, there are few things creepier than watching a Harrowed scuttle up the side of a wall. That’s exactly what this Edge does—it grants the hero the ability to walk on vertical surfaces at their regular Pace. They can even cling to inverted surfaces at half Pace (and they may not run on inverted surfaces).

edges.name: SPIRIT SIGHT
edges.text: As any deader knows, all that power and locomotion is due to a demon squatting inside what’s left of their moldering corpse. Spirit Sight allows the Harrowed to tap into the manitou’s mind for a change, and take a quick gander into the spirit world. (A version of the ability is a modifier to detect arcana, too; see page 179.) Activating Spirit Sight is a free action (but can only be done once per turn if the game is in rounds). This is disorientating so they’re Distracted until the end of turn after they drop the Spirit Sight. While peering into the Hunting Grounds, the Harrowed can view such things as manitous swirling around a huckster or lurking inside the corpse of a walking dead, how twisted an area is (its Fear Level), magical effects on people or objects, or even whether or not a manitou is wriggling around inside of someone. In the latter case, the manitou’s demeanor might even indicate whether it currently controls its Harrowed host. This might allow the deader to notice an invisible creature if it has a spirit (and is thus visible in the spirit world), but doesn’t negate any penalties to affect it. Additionally, any creature with the Fear Special Ability leaves a dark trail through the spirit world. Up to one hour after an abomination has moved through an area, it leaves a faintly glowing spoor of pure evil. A Harrowed with Spirit Sight can use Notice (not Survival in this case) to follow the tainted trail.

edges.name: SPIRIT'S FAVOR
edges.text: (Shaman), Faith d8+ The shaman has gained the favor of a particular spirit and the singular power it grants them. Choose one of the shaman’s powers each time this Edge is taken. The shaman may cast that power as an action without incurring a Multi-Action penalty, allowing them to invoke protection, for example, then make an attack, pray for another blessing, or perform some other action. The shaman may only claim this benefit once per turn, even if they take Spirit’s Favor more than once.

edges.name: SPIRITUAL BARBWIRE
edges.text: This Edge allows a deader to create a barrier that keeps out ghosts, poltergeists, and other ethereal entities—it has no affect on physical entities. The Harrowed makes a Spirit roll and then places a Medium Blast Template centered on themself. The Spiritual Barbwire persists as long as the cowpoke concentrates on it, which inflicts a −2 penalty on other Trait rolls. Entities wishing to enter the Template must make an opposed Spirit check against the deader’s total. If they fail, they cannot pass the barrier while the Edge remains active. Spiritual Barbwire stops the entity from passing through, but does not prevent it from “normal” actions such as Intimidation or throwing physical objects. If any living creature of rat-size or larger that started inside the circle crosses to the outside, the Edge is negated and must be reactivated with another Spirit roll.

edges.name: SPOOK
edges.text: Every so often, an unfortunate soul gets a glimpse of the thing that lives inside a Harrowed. Some run for the hills when they see it. Others might just give a little whimper. But everyone is affected by it, even the most stalwart soul. As an action, a Harrowed can force a single target to make a Fear check at −2. The victim must be reasonably close or able to see the deader (GM’s call), and the power can’t be used on the same target more than once in the same general encounter. The Harrowed can choose to take a level of Fatigue to instead affect all targets within 12” (24 yards).

edges.name: STEADY HANDS
edges.text: Firing from the back of a horse or moving train is tricky business, but your adventurer has figured it out. They ignore the Unstable Platform penalty (page 165). This also helps when running, reducing the usual penalty from −2 to −1 (see Movement, page 146).

edges.name: STITCHIN' (IMP)
edges.text: As above, but the deader rolls every hour.

edges.name: STITCHIN’
edges.text: A dead man with Stitchin’ regenerates much faster than normal—they may make a natural healing roll every day, provided they consume a pound of meat for each attempt.

edges.name: STREETWISE
edges.text: This one knows which saloons to ask questions in and which alleys to avoid. Streetwise characters add +2 to Intimidation or Persuasion rolls made to Network (see page 228) with shady or criminal elements. They also add +2 to Common Knowledge rolls pertaining to the types of disreputable activities listed above.

edges.name: STRONG WILLED
edges.text: When the devil’s whispering and the spirits are wailing, this hombre stands firm. They add +2 to their total when resisting Tests with Smarts or Spirit.

edges.name: SUPERIOR KUNG FU
edges.text: Background (Chi Master), Fighting d8+ Through years of concentrated study under a wizened teacher, your hero has mastered several styles or stances that make up their particular practice of kung fu. Choose one of the options below the first time you take this Edge, and another each additional time you take it. As a free action at the start of their turn, the fighter can assume any one of the styles they’ve taken below. The benefits of the style remain in place until they change to a different one.  DRUNKEN STYLE: The fighter weaves around like they’re out of a tree on fire water, making their moves hard to follow or predict due to a staggering gait. Opponents subtract 2 from attack rolls to hit them, but Pace is reduced by 2 (they may still run).  EAGLE CLAW: The warrior holds her hands like claws, then strikes quickly and viciously at the enemy like a pecking raptor. This gives them unarmed Fighting attacks AP 4 and it’s considered a Heavy Weapon! This ability is critical for those chi masters who find themselves pitted against heavily armored foes, like Dr. Hellstromme’s metal automatons!  MANTIS: A mantis student holds their hands like hooks, moving from mes merizing calm to startling strikes in a terrifying instant. Once per round, anyone who fails a Fighting attack against the martial artist is Distracted or Vulnerable (martial artist’s choice). This is particularly effective when combined with the Counterattack Edge.  MONKEY: The hero shakes their limbs like a primate, contorting and twisting in odd ways that throw off surrounding foes. The martial artist gains +2 Parry, rapidly slapping and blocking away their foes’ strikes. They may also make an Athletics Test against all adjacent foes as a single action. Each one resists separately.  SHUAI CHAO: This form emphasizes light grappling techniques followed by throws or strikes. Once per round, when a foe fails a Fighting attack against the martial artist, they may make a grapple attempt as a free action (see Grappling, page 157).  TAN TUI: The chi master focuses their attack into a powerful snap kick— increasing unarmed combat damage for one Fighting attack per round by one die type. If the attack causes the foe to be Shaken or Wounded, they’re also knocked back 1d4” with success, or 1d4+2” with a raise. With a successful Athletics roll, they can also rise from being prone without costing the usual 2” of movement.  WING CHUN: Wing Chun focuses on fast blocks and flexibility against attacks, like bamboo before a storm. This gives the warrior +1 Parry and subtracts 2 from any melee damage they take while using this style.

edges.name: SUPERNATURAL ATTRIBUTE
edges.text: Supernatural Attribute immediately improves any one attribute by two die types (e.g., a d12 becomes d12+2). This Edge may be taken up to five times, once for each attribute. This increases the limit for that Trait (and any linked skills) a like amount.

edges.name: SWEEP
edges.text: With a mighty swing, this warrior strikes everyone in reach—friend or foe! As a limited action, Sweep allows a character to make a single Fighting attack with a two-handed weapon and apply it against all targets in their Reach (friends and foes alike). Resolve damage separately for each enemy that’s hit. A Sweep made without a two-handed weapon suffers a −2 penalty.

edges.name: SWEEP (IMP)
edges.text: As above but the whirlwind of death is able to avoid allies when using Sweep.

edges.name: TACTICIAN
edges.text: Tacticians read the battlefield like an old dime novel. The commander has a natural grasp of small unit tactics and can take advantage of rapidly changing situations. A Tactician is dealt an extra Action Card each round of combat or a chase—kept separate from their own cards. At the start of the round, they may discard it or give it to any Extra (or group of Extras sharing an Action Card) in Command Range. The player or GM controlling the receiving character or group can decide whether to accept and replace their current Action Card, or discard it.
edges.requirements: Seasoned, Smarts d8+, Command, Battle d6+

edges.name: TALE-TELLER
edges.text: Persuasion d8+ A good storyteller not only entertains, they give hope and comfort as well. In the Weird West, Tale-Tellers are critical to saving the world! What? The world needs saving? You bet it does. Spreading the tales of your posse’s derring-do is far more important in the grand scheme of things than putting down some ornery varmint. So if you do something amazing, bucko, tell people about it! This Edge gives you two perks. First, when making a Persuasion or Performance roll to lower the local Fear Level, your hero adds +2 to their total. Second, when you successfully lower the local Fear Level and get a raise on the Persuasion or Performance roll, the tale- teller and anyone who Supports them earns Conviction (see page 218).

edges.name: TERRITORIAL RANGER
edges.text: United States Marshals police the states. Rangers are responsible for the eight territories—Arizona, California, Idaho, Montana, New Mexico, Washington, Wyoming, the District of Alaska—and one state, Texas, given that organization’s long history there. These law dogs hunt thieves, bandits, deserters, and other fugitives from justice throughout the territories. The Tombstone Epitaph claims they often hunt stranger prey— but only crackpots believe those bedtime stories, right? There’s more information about these tough hombres on page 94.
edges.requirements: Novice, Vigor d6+, Fighting d6+, Intimidation d6+, Riding d6+, Shooting d6+, Survival d4+

edges.name: THIEF
edges.text: Call ‘em grifters, second-story men, or tomb robbers—they’re all good at getting in and out unseen. Thieves add +1 to Athletics (climbing) and Stealth rolls in urban areas. Not surprisingly, thieves are also adept at Thievery itself, adding +1 to those rolls in all circumstances.
edges.requirements: Novice, Agility d8+, Stealth d6+, Thievery d6+

edges.name: TOUGH AS NAILS
edges.text: Your character keeps going when others fall. They can take four Wounds before they’re Incapacitated (the maximum Wound penalty is still −3).

edges.name: TOUGHER THAN NAILS
edges.text: The hero can take up to five Wounds before they’re Incapacitated! The maximum Wound penalty is still −3.
edges.requirements: Legendary, Tough as Nails, Vigor d12+

edges.name: TRACKIN’ TEETH
edges.text: The dead tend to lose body parts here and there. Those with this Edge can keep track of those parts, whether they’re attached to the rest of their cadaver or not! Trackin’ Teeth is a bit of a misnomer as it actually applies to any part of the deader’s body, but this is what Coot Jenkins called it and the name stuck. A clever Harrowed can learn to use it to not only keep track of their parts, but their enemies’ whereabouts as well. They need simply plant a substantial piece of themselves in or on a thing or person. By “substantial” we mean a piece of durable body matter such as a chunk of bone or tooth, not something comparatively insubstantial or perishable, like hair or a scrap of rotten flesh. The most accessible parts of a Harrowed are teeth— hence the Edge’s name. As long as the Harrowed’s piece—tooth or otherwise—is within 10 miles, they can automatically sense its direction and approximate distance. If the piece moves out of range, the Harrowed loses track of it, but they pick it up if it comes back in range again.

edges.name: TRADEMARK WEAPON
edges.text: weapon of d8+ The hero knows one unique weapon, usually given an affectionate name, like the back of their hand. When using it, they add +1 to their Athletics (throwing), Fighting, or Shooting rolls, and +1 to Parry when readied (even if it’s a ranged weapon). A fighter can take this Edge multiple times, applying it to a different weapon each time. If a Trademark Weapon is lost, they can replace it but the benefits don’t kick in for a few days (however long the GM feels is dramatically appropriate).

edges.name: TRUE BELIEVER
edges.text: Background (Blessed), Faith d6+ This holy roller seems to have the ear of their deity. They get a free reroll on Faith rolls.

edges.name: TRUE GENIUS
edges.text: (Mad Scientist) Some say the New Science is inspired by supernatural entities. Most inventors call that superstitious poppycock, but a true genius not only accepts it, they embrace it! After all, it doesn’t matter where the idea comes from, it’s what you do with the technology that matters! Right? Anytime you have to use the Madness Table or infernal device Malfunction Table, you can spend a Benny to have the Marshal roll again, then choose the result you prefer. You may spend as many Bennies as you like until you’re out or as satisfied with the result as you’re gonna get! EXAMPLE: DOC GORDO Doc Samantha “Sam” Gordon needs to cast spiders. She doesn’t have that particular p antes up a Benny and makes an Occult ro card. She’s in a scrapyard full of metal so an ounce of ghost rock for one more card. a Joker, gets a Full House! The Joker gives h 10 Power Points and double damage! Sam needs three Power Points for the spe Blast Template, +1), and Damage (+2) for remaining three Power Points from her Ful −2 for it being a Rank above her (she’s a N Science skill and with the bonus gets an 8! T for a whopping 4d6 damage—doubled afte

edges.name: TRUE GRIT
edges.text: This grizzled veteran has seen things that’d make others’ eyes pop like they just saw a rattler in their bedroll. They ignore all penalties when making Fear checks, and if failed, get one free reroll on the Fear Effects Table if they choose.

edges.name: TWO-FISTED
edges.text: If a character makes a Fighting attack with one action and another from a different hand in a later action, the second attack doesn’t inflict a Multi-Action penalty. The Off- Hand penalty still applies unless they’re Ambidextrous, however (page 38). If the character has Two-Gun Kid, the second action may also be a ranged attack.

edges.name: TWO-GUN KID
edges.text: Two-Gun Kid works just like Two-Fisted, but with ranged weapons, allowing a shooter to fire or throw a weapon in each hand as two different actions but without triggering a Multi-Action penalty. If the character has Two-Fisted, the second action may also be a melee attack. Example: Red has a Bowie knife in one hand and a pistol in the other. She has both Two- Fisted and Two-Gun Kid, so she can make a Fighting attack on one action and then a second Fighting or Shooting attack with no Multi-Action penalty on a later action that turn.

edges.name: UNHOLY HOST
edges.text: This Edge grants the Harrowed a group of five allied Extras. But in this case, the allies are all dead…well, undead to be exact. The host consists of five Walkin’ Dead (see page 327). They’re animated by lesser manitous, who serve as ruthless and chaotic allies. They can speak (though it’s hoarse, gravelly, and stuttering), use weapons, or do anything else a normal person can do. Remember that walkin’ dead in Deadlands aren’t mindless zombies—they’re human husks occupied by lesser demons. The hero doesn’t have a mental link with their Unholy Host, but when they give ‘em orders, the host is bound to follow. Of course they’re also evil incarnate and clever in their interpretations. Give them an inch and they’ll leave a slew of bloody corpses for a mile. The manitous won’t let their champion die if they can help it—that ends their good times on Earth for a while. They might let them suffer and may get a good laugh out of it though! If any are lost, the Harrowed simply needs a new supply of cadavers to let the manitous back in.

edges.name: US MARSHAL
edges.text: US Marshals and Deputy Marshals have legal and policing authority throughout the United States. They may pursue fugitives into territories, but are expected to cooperate with local Rangers as soon as possible. Your character may be a Deputy US Marshal or US Marshal—your choice. Wearing the badge of either grants +1 to Persuasion and Intimidation rolls within their jurisdiction. Deputy Marshals are appointed by “full” US Marshals and have the Obligation (Minor) Hindrance to uphold and enforce the law. They can call on the US Marshal who appointed them if things get out of hand, though that individual might not be local. Deputy Marshals typically receive $50 a month in salary and fees. US Marshals have the Major version of the Hindrance, and are expected to handle most situations on their own. US Marshals gain and can use Favors just like Agents (see page 66). They start with 1 and can spend up to 4 on a request right from the start. They gain an additional Favor when the party reduces the Fear Level. Marshals are paid $300 a month in salary and fees. You can find more information on Marshals and their duties on page 96.
edges.requirements: Novice, Fighting d4+, Riding d4+, Shooting d4+, Trade (Law) d4+

edges.name: VERY ATTRACTIVE
edges.text: This ain’t just some pretty face—it’s the kind that starts bar fights, breaks hearts, and makes folks forget their own names. When this one enters the room, the whole place takes notice. They increase their Performance and Persuasion bonus to +2.

edges.name: VETERAN O' THE WEIRD WEST
edges.text: Those who’ve traveled the Weird West have seen things most folks shouldn’t. Those who survive are marked by their experiences, but also stronger for them. Veterans o’ the Weird West begin play at Seasoned (or one Rank higher than the rest of the cowpokes in your campaign), which means they gain four extra Advances right off the bat. Go ahead and apply those now. There’s a price, though. When you take this Edge, draw a single card from the Action Deck. Show it to the Marshal and she’ll check the table on page 253 to see just what kind of bad luck your hombre wandered into during their travels. Beware—the results can range from maiming to insanity. Your Marshal has all the details. You’ve been warned, Tex!
edges.requirements: Wild Card, Novice, Spirit d6+, Occult d6+

edges.name: WEAPON MASTER
edges.text: The warrior increases their Parry by +1 and the bonus damage die for Fighting rolls is a d8 instead of a d6 (see Bonus Damage, page 148). They must be armed to gain these benefits, but this includes the Martial Artist Edge, claws, or other abilities that count as weapons.

edges.name: WHATELEY BLOOD
edges.text: (Huckster) Somewhere in your family tree is a crooked branch known as the Whateleys. This twisted family of inbred witches and warlocks is known by arcane types as being powerful— and extremely crazy. Hucksters with Whateley spirit running through their veins have learned “blood magic.” Many of the Whateleys are deformed, although your hero doesn’t have to be (take the appropriate Hindrance if they are). All have some telltale mark—pale skin, jet-black hair, long fingernails, sallow complexion, and so on, and all have green eyes. Whatever mark you choose, there’s something about their tainted blood that puts folks off. That unsettled feeling reduces the huckster’s Persuasion rolls by 1, though many overcome it with other Edges taken separately (Attractive, Charismatic, etc.). Now for the meat of the Edge. A huckster with Whateley Blood can voluntarily suffer a Fatigue level for 5 Power Points, or a Wound for 10. This is done exactly as you’d think— by cutting, carving, or otherwise maiming themselves (as a free action, which makes it pretty messy!). Whateleys are a slippery bunch, so if this Incapacitates the caster they complete their turn before keeling over for a dirt nap.

edges.name: WICHITA WITCH
edges.text: (Witch), Spellcasting d8+ Mina Devlin teaches her orphan girls reading, writing, arithmetic, etiquette, and of course, witchcraft! Her “girls” also learn how to defend themselves, intimidate the rough hired guns they often command, and of course, fight. The trademark black mask, provocative leather outfit, and long whip mark the witch as one of Mina’s witches (whether the character is still with her or not). When fully decked out, they add +1 to Intimidation rolls and +1 to Persuasion rolls to those who might be attracted to them. (They subtract 1 from Persuasion rolls when dealing with authorities or “law and order” types— GM’s call). Wichita witches also learn to charge their whip with violent energy. This costs one Power Point, is a free action, and can be triggered after the witch hits with the whip. If they hit with a raise and spend the Power Point, they can add a bonus die to the damage as usual (instead of only Entangling the foe—see Whips on page 120).

edges.name: WITHER
edges.text: This horrifying Edge lets a deader unnaturally age their victim. As an action, the Harrowed must touch the target and make an opposed Spirit roll. If the undead wins, the victim’s flesh and bone wither and decay, reducing Strength a die type (to a minimum of d4) for one hour. With a raise, both Strength and Vigor are reduced a die type. Multiple uses of Wither on the same target don’t stack, but the Harrowed may make secondary attempts to get the raise effect.

edges.name: WIZARD
edges.text: (Magic), Spellcasting d6+ Raw magic is limited only by the taker’s will and imagination. A Wizard can spend 1 extra Power Point when casting a power to change its Trapping. A fireball (blast) might manifest as a lightning bolt, for example. This can often have important consequences if a foe has a particular resistance or weakness to the spell’s usual Trapping.

edges.name: WOODSMAN
edges.text: These are the loners—scouts, trackers, and quiet types who live by the whisperin’ wind. They are skilled trackers and scouts, and know how to live off the land for months at a time. Woodsmen add +2 to Survival rolls, and Stealth rolls made in the wild (not towns, ruins, or underground).

edges.name: WORK THE CROWD
edges.text: As Work the Room but the hero now adds a third skill die to their Support roll this turn and Supports an additional ally.

edges.name: WORK THE ROOM
edges.text: This hero’s got a voice like honey and presence like a sermon in a revival tent. As a limited action, you can use Work the Room to roll a second skill die when Supporting with Persuasion or Performance. The additional die Supports another ally normally and can apply to any Trait chosen. It need not be the same Trait for both allies.

hindrances.name: AILIN'
hindrances.text: Medicine is a rudimentary science on the frontier, and there are worse ways to die than a severe case of lead poisoning. Your cowpoke suffers from a chronic and at least so far incurable disease of some sort. The Minor version of the Hindrance means you subtract 1 from any roll made to resist Fatigue from any source. Subtract 2 if it’s a Major Hindrance. A Critical Failure on such a roll means things are getting worse. If your pistolero has the Minor version, they get worse and the Hindrance becomes Major. If they already have the Major version, the Reaper comes calling. The good news is you gain an immediate point of Conviction. The bad news is you choose when and how your hero dies during that session. They might go out in a blaze of glory or surrounded by friends on a peaceful mountaintop. When they finally pass, the other player characters gain a point of Conviction, drawing strength from the brave death of their stalwart companion. You can also buy off your Hindrance by spending an Advance (two for the Major version of the Hindrance). You should work with the Marshal to figure out a narrative reason for the improvement—treatment at a sanatorium, a miracle cure, a transfusion from a unique donor, or some other story- based explanation for the character’s miraculous improvement.

hindrances.name: ALL THUMBS
hindrances.text: Not everyone takes to the gear-grinding wizardry of infernal devices—or even a basic six-shooter. Maybe you’re jinxed, or maybe you’ve got the Devil’s own luck around anything with moving parts. All Thumbs inflicts a −2 penalty when using mechanical or infernal devices. If they roll a Critical Failure while using such a device (and it doesn’t already have a built-in effect), it’s broken. If the GM feels it’s appropriate, it can be fixed with a Repair roll and 1d6 hours.

hindrances.name: ANEMIC
hindrances.text: You’ve always been a little pale, a little frail, and quick to tire. Maybe it’s bad blood, or maybe you were touched by something unnatural before you were even born. Either way, you’re more likely to wilt when the heat’s on, the chill sets in, or the trail gets rough. You’re the first to sweat, shiver, or swoon when things go south. They subtract 2 from Vigor rolls made to resist Fatigue (see Hazards, starting on page 220).

hindrances.name: ARROGANT
hindrances.text: There’s nobody better than you—and you’re not shy about saying so. You aren’t just good, you’re the best, and you aim to prove it every chance you get. You don’t just want to win, you want your enemies to know they were beat by someone superior. You’ll face the toughest hombres head-on, and if they ain’t ready you’ll wait till they are. It’s pride before the fall, sure, but you’ll never fall, right?

hindrances.name: BAD EYES
hindrances.text: Your peepers just aren’t what they used to be— or maybe they were never right to begin with. You might be nearsighted, farsighted, or just cursed with eyes that don’t pick out a buzzard on a cactus till it’s flapping in your face. Your hombre suffers a −1 penalty to any Trait roll dependent on vision (such as ranged attacks and Notice rolls) or −2 as a Major Hindrance. Glasses are available in the Weird West, at least in major cities. They negate the penalty when worn, but if lost or broken during a combat (generally a 50% chance when your hero is Wounded, falls, or suffers some other trauma), they’re Distracted (and Vulnerable if a Major Hindrance) until the end of their next turn.

hindrances.name: BAD LUCK
hindrances.text: You were born under a bad sign—maybe a blood moon, an eclipsed sun, or your ma crossed a mysterious wanderer and your pa shot a preacher. Whatever the reason, Lady Luck just don’t smile your way. Things go wrong around you more often than not, and fortune always seems to favor the other fella. Your character gets one less Benny per game session than normal, and cannot have both Bad Luck and the Luck Edge.

hindrances.name: BIG MOUTH
hindrances.text: You couldn’t keep a secret if your life depended on it—which, in the Weird West, it often does. The blabbermouth can’t keep a secret very well. They reveal plans and give away things best kept among friends, usually at the worst possible times.

hindrances.name: BLIND
hindrances.text: You can’t see a lick—not the color of the sky, the twitch of a duelist’s hand, or the glow of a haint straight from Hell. The individual is completely without sight and suffers a −6 to all physical tasks that require vision (GM’s call). On the plus side, Blind characters gain their choice of a free Edge to compensate for this particularly difficult Hindrance.

hindrances.name: BLOODTHIRSTY
hindrances.text: Mercy’s for preachers and poets. You don’t take prisoners, and you sure as hell don’t let ‘em walk away. The world’s too cruel for soft hearts, and you reckon a dead enemy won’t stab you in the back later. Of course, that ruthlessness has a price—burned bridges, lost information, and a reputation that draws lawdogs and bounty hunters like flies to a carcass.

hindrances.name: CAN’T SWIM
hindrances.text: Most people in the 19th century can’t swim. Even most sailors are strangers to the water. Your hombre’s one of those. Whether it’s the ocean, a river, or a deep washbasin, they sinks like a stone. Characters with this Hindrance suffer a −2 penalty to the Athletics skill when swimming and each inch moved in water costs 3″ of Pace. See Movement (page 146) for more details and Drowning (221).

hindrances.name: CAUTIOUS
hindrances.text: You ain’t the leap-before-you-look type. Every decision’s got to be chewed on, weighed, and double-checked. Your hero never makes rash decisions and likes to plot things out in detail long before any action is taken.

hindrances.name: CLUELESS
hindrances.text: You wouldn’t notice a ghost if it danced a jig on your hat. You’re a few cards short of a full deck when it comes to paying attention to what’s going on around you. Maybe it’s naivety, maybe you’re just lost in your own world—but in the Weird West, ignorance ain’t bliss. It’s fatal. Your character subtracts 1 from Common Knowledge and Notice rolls.

hindrances.name: CLUMSY
hindrances.text: You’ve got two left feet, a twitchy trigger finger, and all the grace of a newborn calf. Whether you’re trying to sneak through a haunted crypt or just saddle a horse, odds are you’ll trip, fall, or knock something over. Subtle, you ain’t. Subtract 2 from Athletics and Stealth rolls.

hindrances.name: CODE OF HONOR
hindrances.text: You live by a code carved deep in your bones. You don’t break your word, don’t shoot folks in the back, and treat prisoners with dignity. In a land ruled by six-guns and shadows, your honor shines like a lantern in the dark.

hindrances.name: CURIOUS
hindrances.text: You can’t leave well enough alone. Strange tracks? Gotta follow ’em. Locked door? Gotta pick it. Whispered tales of ghost-rock rituals in the hills? Well, now you have to see for yourself. The Weird West is full of things that bite, burn, and beguile—but that never stopped you before.

hindrances.name: CURSED
hindrances.text: Everybody’s got skeletons in the closet, but yours are trying to claw their way out! Your hero has done somebody wrong, either through past affiliation or dark, unspoken deeds. For each player character with the Cursed Hindrance, the GM starts with one additional Benny!

hindrances.name: DEATH WISH
hindrances.text: You aren’t looking to kick the bucket, but you sure wouldn’t mind if it happened while doing something important. Maybe it’s revenge, redemption, or proving a point—but there’s something deep in your heart that makes you charge into danger with a grin and a shrug. Having a death wish doesn’t mean your adventurer is suicidal—they might just think their life is worth less than some noble but clearly deadly goal. Those with a Death Wish don’t throw their lives away for no reason, but when there’s a chance to complete a goal they do anything— and take any risk—to achieve it.

hindrances.name: DELUSIONAL
hindrances.text: Your hero believes something considered strange by everyone else. Minor Delusions are harmless or the character generally keeps it to themself (President Lincoln is still alive and runs the United States Agency, the moon is made of cheese, we’re all just characters in some bizarre game, and so on). With a Major Delusion, your character expresses their view on the situation frequently and it can occasionally lead to danger (the walkin’ dead are just misunderstood, all machines are the Devil’s handiwork, I’m immune to bullets while wearing my grandfather’s badge).

hindrances.name: DOUBTING THOMAS
hindrances.text: Some people don’t believe in the supernatural until they’re halfway down some creature’s gullet. Doubting Thomases are skeptics who try their best to rationalize supernatural events. They walk right into danger they don’t believe in and look for alternate explanations to every supernatural event. Even after being confronted with undeniable truth, the doubter’s mind eventually begins to doubt what they saw, rationalizes it away, or compartmentalizes the event as “one of a kind” while continuing to doubt the next mystery.

hindrances.name: DRIVEN
hindrances.text: You’ve got a goal, and come Hell or high water, you’re gonna reach it. Maybe you want to prove the existence of monsters, get revenge on a bandit gang, or write your name in every history book from here to Deseret. The Minor version shapes the character and pushes their decisions but either happens rarely or is fairly harmless. As a Major Hindrance it’s an overriding desire that comes up frequently or causes peril for the character and maybe even the posse!

hindrances.name: ELDERLY
hindrances.text: Your adventurer is getting on in years, but they’re not quite ready for Boot Hill yet. Their Pace is reduced by 1 and they subtract 1 from running rolls (minimum 1). They also take a −1 penalty to Agility, Strength (including damage), and Vigor rolls, but not linked skills. On the plus side, the wisdom of their years grants the old timer 5 extra skill points which may be used for any skills linked to Smarts.

hindrances.name: ENEMY
hindrances.text: Someone out there hates your sidewinder and wants ‘em ruined, locked away, or dead. The value of the Hindrance depends on how powerful the enemy is and how often they might show up. A Minor Enemy might be a lone gunslinger out for vengeance or a betrayed brotherhood that’s deadly but appears rarely. A Major Enemy might represent powerful authorities like the Agency, a band of outlaws, or a single powerful and relentless rival. If the enemy is one day defeated, the GM should gradually work in a replacement, or the hero may buy off the Hindrance by sacrificing an Advance.

hindrances.name: GREEDY
hindrances.text: Gold, ghost rock, or even a fancy pair of boots—if it’s worth something, you want it. Maybe you grew up dirt-poor, maybe you just think you deserve more than the rest, or maybe something deeper and darker drives that hunger for wealth. If a Minor Hindrance, they argue bitterly for more than their fair share of any loot or reward the party might come across. As a Major Hindrance, they fight over anything they consider unfair, and may even kill for it if they feel slighted or covet something they can’t have.

hindrances.name: GRIM SERVANT O' DEATH
hindrances.text: Only Wild Cards can take this Hindrance, and you shouldn’t do it lightly, amigo. Your hero’s a killer. Their family’s probably pushing up daisies, their enemies are worm food, and even a few of “friends” have holes in them that are suspiciously the same caliber as your very own shootin’ iron. The good news is your hombre adds +1 to every damage roll they ever make, whether it’s from Fighting, Shooting, an arcane skill roll, or even using Athletics to throw things at people in a most inhospitable manner. The downside is your malcontent winds up in the hoosegow or on the run from his enemies a lot. Worse, anytime their attack roll is a Critical Failure, they hit the nearest ally in sight—with a raise! This happens whether the target’s in the line of fire or not. Maybe the killer’s gun hand gets jostled, the bullet ricochets, or they catch flying shrapnel from an explosion. Other players’ characters are always first choice, but any friendly soul will do in a pinch. Even hand-to-hand attacks hit allies when a Grim Servant o’ Death gets violent. This may require a little imagination, but either the weapon flies out of the hero’s hand and strikes their friend, or the hero moves adjacent to an erstwhile amigo and “accidentally” whacks ‘em. Even if you’re using miniatures, combat is more fluid than the tabletop depicts.

hindrances.name: HABIT
hindrances.text: Your cowpoke has an annoying or dangerous compulsion. A Minor Habit irritates those around them but isn’t dangerous. Maybe they pick their nose, can’t stop fiddling with their pocket watch, curses even in polite company, or chews and spits tobacco everywhere. A Major Habit is a physical or mental addiction of some sort that is debilitating or possibly even deadly. This includes drug use and chronic drinking. An addict who doesn’t get their fix must make a Vigor roll every 24 hours they go without or take a level of Fatigue (see page 156). Once every 24 hours, a Healing roll with some sort of appropriate medicine removes one level of Fatigue for four hours. After that the Fatigue returns and can only be recovered with the addicting substance.

hindrances.name: HARD OF HEARING
hindrances.text: Gunshots, thunder, and the wailing of things best left unnamed can leave a soul hard of hearing. As a Minor Hindrance, those who have lost some or all of their subtract 4 from all Notice rolls made to hear, including awaking due to loud noises. A Major Hindrance means the character is deaf. They cannot hear and automatically fail all Notice rolls that depend on hearing.

hindrances.name: HEAVY SLEEPER
hindrances.text: Your cowboy drops off like they’ve been hit with a sledgehammer—and ain’t much wakes them once they’re out. Gunfire, screamin’, thunderin’ hooves—it’s all just background noise to this dreamer. Problem is, when the nightmares come—and in the Weird West, they do—they might not wake up ‘til it’s too late. Once they drop off, they must make a Notice roll (−4) to wake up. They also suffers a −4 penalty to Vigor rolls made to stay awake.

hindrances.name: HEROIC
hindrances.text: This noble soul never says no to a person in need. They don’t have to be happy about it, but they come to the rescue of those they feel can’t help themselves. They’re the first one to run into a burning building, usually agree to hunt monsters for little to no pay, and generally a pushover for a sob story.

hindrances.name: HESITANT
hindrances.text: When bullets start flyin’ and blood hits the dirt, some folks freeze. Maybe it’s nerves, maybe they’re thinking too hard. Either way, this cowpoke’s slow on the draw, which can make the difference between a grave and a tale worth tellin’. Draw two Action Cards in combat and act on the lowest. If you draw a Joker, use it normally and ignore the Hindrance for the round (hence this being a Minor Hindrance, it actually increases your chances of drawing a Joker!) Hesitant characters cannot take the Quick or Level Headed Edges.

hindrances.name: ILLITERATE
hindrances.text: Your hero cannot read. They can sign their name and know a sign says SALOON or LIVERY, but not much else. They also doesn’t know much about math. They can probably do 2 + 2 = 4, but multiplication and the like are beyond ‘em. Illiterate characters can’t read or write in any language, by the way, no matter how many they actually speak.

hindrances.name: IMPULSIVE
hindrances.text: This hombre’s got a streak of wild lightning in ‘im. See a locked door? Kick it in. Hear a spooky tale? Go check it out. Whether it’s bravery or bull-headedness is up for debate, but one thing’s for sure—this impulsive soul charges headfirst into trouble, usually without asking how deep the water is.

hindrances.name: JEALOUS
hindrances.text: The green-eyed monster rides heavy on this one’s shoulders. Maybe it’s just a simmerin’ grudge when someone else gets praised, or maybe it’s a full-blown obsession with takin’ what ain’t theirs. In a land where reputation can mean life or death, envy’s a dangerous poison. As a Minor Hindrance, the character’s jealousy is focused on one particular subject (such as their “unrivaled” skill as a gunslinger or a romantic interest). As a Major Hindrance, the character is jealous of anyone and everyone they feel outshines them. They consistently bad- mouth their rivals, try to upstage them, or actively plot to discredit those who threaten their ego.

hindrances.name: LOYAL
hindrances.text: In the Weird West, trust is rarer than a dry match in a flood. That’s what makes your hero different. Whether it’s blood ties or battlefield bonds, they stand by their companions no matter the odds. They might grumble or play it off, but if you’re in trouble, they’re comin’—six-gun in hand and fire in their heart.

hindrances.name: LYIN’ EYES
hindrances.text: This poor soul just isn’t cut out for bluffing. Maybe it’s the twitchy hands, the shifty eyes, or the stammering voice—but whatever it is, folks can smell a fib the minute it leaves their lips. That makes bluffing in a poker game mighty difficult—and talking your way outta trouble near impossible. A hero with this Hindrance suffers a −1 penalty to all Intimidation and Persuasion rolls where lies—even little ones— must be told. Worse, if your hero plans to make money playing poker, the penalty also applies to bluffing. That’s −1 to your Gambling rolls in a poker or faro game as well, compadre!

hindrances.name: MEAN
hindrances.text: Some folks are just born ornery. This one scowls at charity, sneers at good deeds, and spits venom every chance they get. They aren’t necessarily evil—but they sure aren’t friendly either, and kindness seems like a foreign language to ‘em. Besides the obvious roleplaying issues, Mean characters subtract 1 from Persuasion rolls.

hindrances.name: MILD MANNERED
hindrances.text: Not everyone looks like they belong in a showdown at high noon. This tenderfoot has a soft voice, gentle ways, and an aura that screams “not a threat.” Whatever the issue, they have a hard time looking tough. They subtracts 2 when making Intimidation rolls.

hindrances.name: MUTE
hindrances.text: Speech is silver, silence is gold—but for your cowgirl, it’s the only option. Whether by birth, trauma, or a dark deal gone wrong, they can’t speak a word. They rely on notes, signs, or cold stares to get their point across, and when things go south, they better hope actions speak louder than words. Your heroine can write messages to others when needed, use sign language (yes, it exists at this time), or some combination of visual communication. Vision-based communication may require a Notice roll to perceive correctly (illumination and similar penalties apply).

hindrances.name: NIGHT TERRORS
hindrances.text: The prospect of sleep is a constant dread for your sidewinder. They toss and turn like a demon on a rack, and likely keep everyone within earshot awake with their nightly torments. The repeated barrage on their psyche results in an overall weakened resolve. They subtract 1 from all Spirit rolls.

hindrances.name: OBESE
hindrances.text: Your hero’s built more like a chuckwagon than a mustang. Those who carry their weight well have the Brawny Edge. Those who don’t are Obese. A character cannot be both Brawny and Obese, and this Hindrance can’t increase your Size above +3. An Obese hero’s Size (and therefore Toughness) increases by +1. Their Pace is reduced by 1, and their running die one die type (minimum d4). Strength is considered one die type less (minimum d4) for armor and worn gear (not weapons). They may also have difficulty finding armor or clothing that fits or entering confined spaces.

hindrances.name: OBLIGATION
hindrances.text: Your hero has a responsibility they must attend to on a daily or regular basis. It could be a job, volunteer work for the local church, taking care of family or friends, etc. The Obligation consumes about 20 hours most weeks, or 40+ for the Major version. Exactly what that entails should be discussed between the player and the Game Master.

hindrances.name: OLD WAYS OATH
hindrances.text: Your hero has pledged to forego modern technology to honor the nature spirits. Those who remain true to their vows get a free reroll on any Spirit roll. If the character violates the agreement, however, the spirits withdraw this advantage for 24 hours. If the oath-taker uses an item powered by ghost rock—a noxious and cancerous substance to nature spirits—their support is withdrawn for a week.

hindrances.name: ONE ARM
hindrances.text: By birth or battle, your hero lost an arm. Fortunately, their other arm is (now) their “good” one. Tasks that require two hands, such as some Athletics rolls (GM’s call) or using a two-handed weapon, suffer a −4 modifier.

hindrances.name: ONE EYE
hindrances.text: This veteran lost an eye and has trouble with depth perception. They subtract 2 from any Trait roll dependent on vision and more than 5″ (10 yards) distant.

hindrances.name: OUTSIDER
hindrances.text: In a society made up of only a few types of people, your hero ain’t one of them. A Navajo in Apache lands, a Native American in some Western towns, or a New York dandy on the frontier are all examples. Locals are likely to raise prices on them, ignore pleas for help, and generally treat them as lower class. Outsiders subtract 2 from Persuasion rolls made to influence those who aren’t their own kind.

hindrances.name: OVERCONFIDENT
hindrances.text: Your hero walks into every town like they’re the fastest draw alive and every haunted mine like it’s already cleared. Confidence like that is powerful—but when it isn’t backed up it can lead straight to Boot Hill. They rarely retreat, don’t reconsider, and sure as hell don’t back down unless it absolutely can’t be helped. They’re not suicidal, but they certainly take on more than common sense dictates.

hindrances.name: PACIFIST
hindrances.text: Bloodshed don’t sit right with this one. Whether from religious conviction, a vow made on a battlefield, or just a heart too kind for the times, your hero avoids violence whenever possible. Minor pacifism means the gal only fights when given no other choice and never allows the killing of prisoners or other defenseless victims. Major Pacifists won’t fight living characters under any circumstances. They may defend themselves, but won’t do anything to permanently harm sapient, living creatures. They may use nonlethal methods (see page 160), but only in self-defense or the defense of others. Note that undeniably evil creatures, undead, demons, and the like are fair game even for Major Pacifists!

hindrances.name: PHOBIA
hindrances.text: There’s a shadow in your hero’s soul, something that clutches the heart tight whenever it rears its head. Not a common fear—nothing so simple as being scared of vampires or walking into a haunted mine. No, this is stranger: red candles, hymns, or the smell of sulfur and sage. Phobias are overwhelming and irrational fears that plague a hero’s psyche. Whenever a character is in the presence of their phobia (GM’s call, but generally sight), they subtract 1 from all Trait rolls if it’s a Minor Hindrance, and 2 if it’s Major. Phobias shouldn’t be too obvious; everyone should be afraid of vampires, for example, so that’s not a phobia, it’s common sense. Phobias should be of some random element the mind associates with a traumatic event, like the red candles a vampire burned in its crypt, or the player piano music that played every time a ghost showed itself.

hindrances.name: POVERTY
hindrances.text: Money slips through your cowpoke’s fingers like water in a desert. Maybe they got a taste for drinking, gambling, or just a knack for making bad investments. Or maybe they’re cursed—some folks are. Your hero starts with only $125 (instead of $250) and just can’t seem to hang on to dinero acquired after play begins. In general, the player halves their total funds every game week and is just generally broke.

hindrances.name: QUIRK
hindrances.text: Quirks are minor foibles; usually humorous but can occasionally troublesome. A Sioux warrior might always want to count coup (touch) on a foe before attacking it, a huckster might constantly shuffle their cards, or a snobby débutante might not eat, drink, or socialize with the lower class, for example.

hindrances.name: RUTHLESS
hindrances.text: The fanatic will do most anything to accomplish their goals. As a Minor Hindrance, they stop short of true harm to anyone except those who directly oppose ‘em. As a Major Hindrance, almost nothing gets in their way.

hindrances.name: SECRET
hindrances.text: Everyone’s got skeletons, but your hero’s got one that rattles. Could be they made a deal with a manitou, betrayed their posse, or were involved in a massacre that got hushed up. As a Minor Hindrance, the secret is troublesome but not life-threatening. The Major version would cause severe problems if discovered. If it ever becomes public knowledge, they should trade it for Enemy, Shamed, Wanted, or another appropriate Hindrance approved by the GM.

hindrances.name: SHAMED
hindrances.text: Something haunts your adventurer. Maybe they made a vow they didn’t keep. Maybe they were defeated in an honorable fight and ordered the death of their foe anyway for some greater principle. Maybe they aren’t actually cowardly but once ran from a battle and left others to die. As a Minor Hindrance, the shameful circumstances aren’t generally known—it just haunts the hero. They might go out of their way, against all reason, not to repeat the mistake. Or they might give in to the same set of circumstances and hate themselves for it. As a Major Hindrance, their deed is well- known—or at least known among those they care about. The other player characters should be told the tale as soon as possible (preferably at character creation). If not, it should be revealed by nonplayer characters at some point, and occasionally used against the hero.

hindrances.name: SLOW
hindrances.text: This cowpoke doesn’t move like they used to. Maybe they have a limp from an old war wound, a twisted spine from riding the range too long, or just bad luck with a rattler. As a Minor Hindrance, reduce Pace by 1 and running die one step (if already d4, reduce to d4−1). As a Major Hindrance, reduce the running die a step, Pace by 2, and subtract 2 from Athletics rolls and rolls to resist Athletics (such as Tests or Grappling). Slow characters may not take the Fleet- Footed Edge. Prosthesis: A character with the Minor version of this Hindrance may have a prosthesis. If the prosthesis is lost, they suffer the effects of the Major version of Slow. Wheelchairs: These contraptions are rare on the frontier given the state of most streets and lack of ramps, but they do exist. Slow heroes may start with a manual wheelchair at no cost, but they only help over reasonably smooth ground to operate (GM’s call). Pace in a wheelchair is half the hero’s Athletics die (max of 3) and they cannot run.

hindrances.name: SMALL
hindrances.text: Your cowpoke is knee-high to a grasshopper, or thin as a bean pole. Their Size (see page 18) is reduced by 1, which reduces Toughness by 1 as well. Size can’t be reduced below −1, but the Toughness penalty remains.

hindrances.name: STUBBORN
hindrances.text: Stubborn individuals always want their way and never admit they’re wrong. Even when it’s painfully obvious they’ve made a mistake they try to justify it with half-truths and rationalizations.

hindrances.name: SUSPICIOUS
hindrances.text: Trust is a rare coin, and your hero doesn’t carry any. They eye every partner like a potential backstabber and treat every deal like a con. As a Minor Hindrance, their paranoia causes frequent trust issues. They might demand full payment before doing a task, want every agreement in writing, or believe even their friends are out to get them. As a Major Hindrance, Support rolls to aid the distrustful individual are made at −2.

hindrances.name: TALISMAN
hindrances.text: Your spell-slinger’s tied their mojo to a single item—a charm, deck, amulet, or relic. Anyone who sees the item used to enact a power can tell it’s important. Only characters with an Arcane Background Edge can take this Hindrance. It represents a mental dependence on a physical item to use their powers. The Talisman could be a specific deck of cards for a huckster, a medicine bag for a shaman, a holy item for a blessed, or a unique weapon for a chi master. Whatever the item, the character suffers a −1 penalty to all arcane skill rolls if they don’t have it on their person. As a Major Hindrance, they suffer a −2 without it. The hero can replace a lost Talisman, but it takes two game weeks to acclimate to the replacement, during which time the hombre suffers the appropriate penalties. Note that mad scientists already need a chosen gizmo to enact powers—an actual dependence rather than a mental one. Therefore, characters with that Arcane Background aren’t eligible for this Hindrance.

hindrances.name: TENDERFOOT
hindrances.text: Every little cut and scrape makes your cowpoke cry for mama. As long as they have at least one Wound, they suffer an additional −1 penalty to all their actions (so a hero with two Wounds has a −3 Wound penalty, for example, although −3 is still the maximum). A hero with this Hindrance can’t take the Don’t Get ’im Riled! Edge.

hindrances.name: THIN SKINNED
hindrances.text: Personal attacks get under your skin like a saddlebur. As a Minor Hindrance, your sidewinder subtracts 2 when resisting Taunt attacks. As a Major, they subtract 4.

hindrances.name: TIMID
hindrances.text: Your hero flinches at loud noises, startles at shadows, and breaks a sweat just drawing a weapon. Violence makes them nauseous and terror sticks to ‘em like grave dust. Not everyone’s meant to be a gunslinger—and this one might not even be meant to watch a fight. They subtract 2 from Fear checks and when resisting Intimidation.

hindrances.name: TONGUE-TIED
hindrances.text: Whether it’s nerves, a stammer, or just a knack for saying the wrong thing, this cowpoke’s words tend to work against them. Sweet-talking, bluffing, even telling a joke— none of it lands right. And don’t even try to impress a crowd unless you want laughter for all the wrong reasons. They suffer a −1 penalty to Intimidation, Performance, Persuasion, and Taunt rolls that involve speech.

hindrances.name: TROUBLE MAGNET
hindrances.text: Bad luck isn’t a rare occurrence for your sodbuster—it’s a lifestlye. As a Minor Hindrance, whenever the character rolls a Critical Failure the consequences are worse in some way. A hero isn’t just spotted trying to infiltrate a US Army fort, someone recognizes their face. A buckaroo doesn’t just fail at Intimidation, the target’s friends take personal offense. Or a botched attack roll results in the cowpoke’s weapon falling apart. The Major Hindrance has a different effect. Anytime the Marshal must choose a “random character” to be hit, attacked, or otherwise negatively affected by something—it’s this poor devil.

hindrances.name: UGLY
hindrances.text: This poor soul’s face could sour milk. They subtract 1 from their Persuasion rolls, or 2 if taken as a Major Hindrance.

hindrances.name: VENGEFUL
hindrances.text: Those who trouble your ornery cuss are in for payback. As a Minor Hindrance they usually seek vengeance legally. The method varies by situation—some plot and scheme for months while others demand immediate results. Those with the Major version of this Hindrance don’t let anything prevent them from a reckoning. This doesn’t mean they immediately resort to violence, but their actions always escalate until total and complete satisfaction is achieved.

hindrances.name: WANTED
hindrances.text: Your hero has committed a crime and will be arrested if discovered by the relevant authorities. The level of the Hindrance depends on how serious the crime was and how active the hunters are. A hero Wanted for robbery in a few towns in the Southwest has a Minor Hindrance. A horse-thief or murderer, or the same thief known and Wanted in the main campaign area, has a Major Hindrance.

hindrances.name: YOUNG
hindrances.text: The hero is 12–15 years old. They only have 4 points to adjust their attributes instead of 5, and 10 skill points instead of 12. On the plus side, youths have a fair amount of luck. They draw one extra Benny at the beginning of each game session (this stacks with other Edges such Luck or Great Luck). Most Young characters should also take the Small Hindrance, but it’s not mandatory. As a Major Hindrance, the character is Very Young (8 to 11 years old). They have only 3 points for attributes and 10 for skills, and the Small Hindrance. Very Young heroes draw two extra Bennies at the start of each session.
